overview.text: **Module objective:** Understand how backend systems work, how applications communicate with servers, how requests are processed, and how to translate application requirements into a backend architecture.

Backend engineering is not simply about writing APIs or connecting a database. It is about designing and building the systems that receive requests, execute business rules, manage data, enforce security, communicate with other services, and return reliable responses.
By the end of this module, you should be able to look at an application such as a learning platform, an e-commerce website, or a banking application and explain what happens behind the interface.

blocks.text: 1.1 Understanding the backend
Consider a student using an online learning platform.
The student opens a course, watches a lesson, marks it as completed, and checks their learning progress.
The student sees buttons, text, videos, progress bars, and menus. These are primarily part of the frontend. But several important operations happen behind the interface:

items: The application checks whether the student is logged in.
It identifies which student is making the request.
It retrieves the course and lesson information.
It checks whether the lesson belongs to that course.
It records that the student completed the lesson.
It calculates the updated course progress.
It sends the updated information back to the frontend.

blocks.text: These operations are handled by the backend.
**Backend engineering** is the discipline of designing, developing, testing, deploying, and maintaining the server-side components of an application.
The backend is responsible for the application's rules, data processing, access control, and communication with other systems.
1.2 The three major parts of an application
A typical application can be understood through three major components:
**Frontend — User Interface**
What the user sees and interacts with
Pages · Forms · Buttons · Dashboards
HTTP / HTTPS requests and responses
**Backend — Application Logic**
Processes requests and enforces business rules
APIs · Authentication · Validation · Services
Database queries and results
**Database — Persistent Storage**
Stores and retrieves application data
Students · Courses · Progress · Transactions
These three components work together, but they have different responsibilities.
**Frontend:** Handles user interactions and presents information. It may perform basic validation for a better user experience, but it cannot be trusted to enforce important security rules.
**Backend:** Receives requests, verifies permissions, runs business logic, coordinates operations, and decides what information to return.
**Database:** Stores information so that it remains available after a user closes the application or a server restarts.
A production system may have additional components, such as a cache, message queue, object storage, search engine, and external services. We will encounter these as the course progresses.
1.3 What responsibilities does a backend perform?
| Responsibility   | What it means                   | Example                           |
| Request handling | Receives client requests        | Student opens a course            |
| Authentication   | Establishes who the user is     | Verify a login session            |
| Authorization    | Determines what the user may do | Only an instructor edits a course |
| Business logic   | Implements application rules    | Calculate course completion       |
| Data management  | Reads and writes information    | Save lesson progress              |
| Validation       | Checks submitted data           | Reject an invalid email           |
| Integration      | Communicates with other systems | Send an email through a provider  |
| Security         | Protects application resources  | Prevent unauthorized access       |
| Reliability      | Handles errors and failures     | Retry a temporary service failure |
| Observability    | Makes system behavior visible   | Record errors and request latency |
1.4 Backend engineering is more than CRUD
CRUD stands for:
For example, a student management system may provide CRUD operations for student records.
However, real backend engineering requires more than CRUD.
Suppose a student submits an assignment. The backend may need to:
1. Confirm the student is authenticated.

sections.title: 2. Verify that the student is enrolled in the course.
5. Verify that the submission deadline has not passed.
7. Record the submission in the database.
9. Return a confirmation to the student.

blocks.text: This process contains authentication, authorization, validation, business logic, file storage, database operations, and external communication.
That is why backend development requires system thinking, not simply endpoint creation.
1.5 A practical example: Mark a lesson as completed
Imagine the frontend sends this request:

POST /api/v1/lessons/lesson-101/complete
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Content-Type: application/json
The backend may perform the following operations:

1. Receive the request.
2. Validate the access token.
3. Identify the student.
4. Find lesson-101.
5. Verify course enrollment.
6. Check whether the lesson can be completed.
7. Save the completion record.
8. Recalculate course progress.
9. Return the result.
Example response:
The frontend can now update the progress bar to 25%.
Notice an important design principle: the frontend does not decide that the student has completed 25% of the course. The backend calculates this using the actual records and the application's rules.
1.6 Where does backend code run?
Backend applications run in server-side runtime environments.
Examples include:
| Runtime or platform        | Purpose                                |
| Node.js                    | Runs JavaScript outside the browser    |
| Java Virtual Machine (JVM) | Executes Java applications             |
| .NET runtime               | Executes supported .NET applications   |
| Python runtime             | Executes Python applications           |
| Go runtime environment     | Runs compiled Go applications          |
| Cloudflare Workers runtime | Runs applications at Cloudflare's edge |
A backend does not necessarily need to run on a traditional physical server. It can run on a virtual machine, a container platform, a serverless platform, or an edge runtime.
The important distinction is its responsibility: it executes server-side application logic and responds to requests.
1.7 Important terminology
**API:** A defined interface that allows one software system to communicate with another.
**Endpoint:** A particular API address and method combination, such as `GET /api/v1/courses`.
**Request:** Information sent to a server by a client.
**Response:** Information returned by the server.
**Business logic:** Rules that describe how an application is supposed to behave.
**Persistence:** The ability to retain data beyond the lifetime of a single operation or process.
**Scalability:** The ability of a system to handle increasing workloads by using available resources effectively.
**Availability:** The extent to which a system is accessible and functioning when users need it.

sections.title: 2. Frontend vs Backend vs Full-Stack Architecture

blocks.text: 2.1 Understanding the distinction
A modern application generally has a client-facing layer and a server-side layer. Developers may specialize in one layer or work across both.
**Frontend development** focuses on the user experience and interface.
**Backend development** focuses on server-side behavior, data, application rules, and integrations.
**Full-stack development** involves working across the frontend and backend, understanding how the two communicate and fit together.
These are different responsibilities, but they are not isolated disciplines.
2.2 Frontend architecture
The frontend is the part of an application that users interact with directly.
For a web application, it usually runs inside a browser.
Its responsibilities include:

items: Managing loading, success, and error states.
Providing an accessible and responsive user experience.

blocks.text: A React application, for example, might contain:

Frontend Application
│
├── Pages
│   ├── LoginPage
│   ├── DashboardPage
│   └── CoursePage
│
├── Components
│   ├── Navbar
│   ├── CourseCard
│   └── ProgressBar
│
├── Services
│   ├── authService
│   └── courseService
│
├── State Management
│
└── Routing
The frontend should not contain secret API keys, database credentials, or authoritative permission rules. Browser code is accessible to the user and should be treated as an untrusted environment.
2.3 Backend architecture
The backend runs in a server-side environment.
Its responsibilities include:
A backend project might be organized as follows:

Backend Application
│
├── Routes
│   ├── authRoutes
│   ├── studentRoutes
│   └── courseRoutes
│
├── Controllers
│   ├── authController
│   ├── studentController
│   └── courseController
│
├── Services
│   ├── authService
│   ├── studentService
│   └── courseService
│
├── Repositories
│   ├── studentRepository
│   └── courseRepository
│
├── Middleware
│   ├── authentication
│   ├── authorization
│   └── errorHandler
│
├── Database
│
└── Configuration
This is one possible organization, not a universal requirement. Small applications may use fewer layers. Larger systems may separate responsibilities even further.
2.4 Full-stack architecture
A full-stack application connects the frontend, backend, and storage layers into one working system.
Consider a student dashboard.
| User action       | Frontend responsibility             | Backend responsibility                      |
| Log in            | Collect credentials and submit them | Verify credentials and establish a session  |
| View courses      | Request and display courses         | Verify access and retrieve courses          |
| Open a lesson     | Display lesson content              | Return permitted lesson content             |
| Complete a lesson | Send completion request             | Validate and save completion                |
| View progress     | Display progress data               | Calculate and return authoritative progress |
| Update profile    | Collect edits and display result    | Validate and persist permitted changes      |
The frontend manages presentation; the backend manages trusted application behavior.

2.6 Comparison: Frontend vs Backend vs Full-Stack
| Area                    | Frontend                           | Backend                                   | Full-stack                         |
| Primary focus           | User interface                     | Server-side systems                       | Complete application               |
| Main environment        | Browser                            | Server or managed runtime                 | Both                               |
| Typical technologies    | React, Vue, Angular                | Java, Node.js, Python, Go                 | Combination                        |
| Main interfaces         | UI components                      | APIs and services                         | UI and APIs                        |
| Data responsibility     | Display and temporary state        | Trusted data processing                   | End-to-end data flow               |
| Security responsibility | Safe handling of user interactions | Authentication, authorization, validation | Understanding security across both |
| Testing                 | UI and component tests             | API, integration, and service tests       | End-to-end and component tests     |
2.7 A crucial distinction: frontend validation vs backend validation
Suppose a registration form asks for a student's age.
The frontend checks whether the entered value is a positive number. This improves usability by giving immediate feedback.
But a user can modify browser code or send an HTTP request without using the interface.
Therefore, the backend must validate the age again before accepting the registration.
The general rule is:
**Frontend validation improves the experience. Backend validation protects the system.**
The same principle applies to prices, permissions, enrollment status, discounts, file uploads, and other important business rules.
2.8 When is each specialization useful?
Choose frontend specialization when your main interest is interface engineering, visual systems, accessibility, and user experience.
Choose backend specialization when you are interested in APIs, data architecture, algorithms, security, distributed systems, and server-side reliability.

Choose full-stack development when you want to build complete features across the interface and server layers. Full-stack development does not mean that you must be equally expert in every area; it means you understand how the complete application works.

3.1 What is client-server architecture?
Client-server architecture is a computing model in which one component, called the client, requests a service or resource, and another component, called the server, provides it.
The client initiates communication. The server processes the request and provides a response.
For example, when a student opens PrepSpaces in a browser:

items: The browser acts as the client.
The backend application acts as the server.
The browser and backend communicate through HTTP or HTTPS.
The backend communicates with the database using its database interface or driver.

blocks.text: The client-server model is not limited to websites. Mobile applications, desktop applications, payment systems, and other software can use the same model.
3.2 Understanding the client
A client is a software component that requests a resource or operation from another system.
Common examples include:
| Client              | Example                                         |
| Web browser         | Chrome requesting a dashboard                   |
| Mobile application  | Android app requesting account details          |
| Desktop application | Desktop email client retrieving messages        |
| Command-line tool   | `curl` requesting an API                        |
| Another backend     | Payment service requesting customer information |
A client typically knows:

items: The authentication information needed to make the request.

blocks.text: A client should not need to know the private internal implementation of the server.
For example, the frontend does not need to know whether the backend uses Java, Node.js, or Python. It only needs to follow the API contract.
3.3 Understanding the server
A server is a software system that listens for requests and provides services to clients.
A backend server may:
2. Identify the requested operation.
3. Authenticate the requester.
4. Verify permissions.
5. Execute application logic.
6. Retrieve or modify data.
7. Return a response.
A server is not necessarily one physical computer. It may be software running inside a container, a virtual machine, a serverless environment, or a distributed cloud infrastructure.
3.4 How client and server communicate
Web applications commonly communicate using HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol).
HTTP defines how clients and servers exchange requests and responses.
An HTTP request commonly contains:
| Component | Purpose                                        |
| Method    | Describes the requested operation              |
| URL       | Identifies the destination resource            |
| Headers   | Provide metadata and other request information |
| Body      | Contains optional data sent to the server      |
Example request:

POST /api/v1/students HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>

{
  "name": "Rahul Sharma",
  "email": "rahul@example.com",
  "department": "Computer Science"
}
In this example:

items: The JSON body contains the student information.

blocks.text: The server may return:
`201 Created` indicates that the server successfully created a resource.
3.5 HTTP methods
HTTP methods communicate the intended operation.
| Method | Typical purpose                           | Example                            |
| GET    | Retrieve a resource                       | `GET /api/v1/students`             |
| POST   | Create a resource or perform an operation | `POST /api/v1/students`            |
| PUT    | Replace a resource representation         | `PUT /api/v1/students/stu-1001`    |
| PATCH  | Partially update a resource               | `PATCH /api/v1/students/stu-1001`  |
| DELETE | Delete a resource                         | `DELETE /api/v1/students/stu-1001` |
Consider the difference between PUT and PATCH.
A PUT request may send a complete replacement representation:
PUT /api/v1/students/stu-1001
A PATCH request may update only one field:
PATCH /api/v1/students/stu-1001
An important HTTP concept is **idempotency**.
An operation is idempotent when repeating the same request has the same intended effect on the server as performing it once.
For example, setting a student's department to Information Technology using a PUT request is generally idempotent. Repeating that update should not keep creating new records.
A POST request that creates a new student is generally not idempotent: repeating it may create multiple students unless the application implements duplicate protection or an idempotency mechanism.
3.6 Understanding HTTP status codes
The server uses status codes to communicate the outcome of a request.
| Code | Meaning               | Common scenario                               |
| 200  | OK                    | Data retrieved successfully                   |
| 201  | Created               | Student created                               |
| 204  | No Content            | Successful operation with no response body    |
| 400  | Bad Request           | Invalid request data                          |
| 401  | Unauthorized          | Missing or invalid authentication             |
| 403  | Forbidden             | Authenticated but insufficient permission     |
| 404  | Not Found             | Requested student does not exist              |
| 409  | Conflict              | Duplicate or conflicting operation            |
| 422  | Unprocessable Content | Request content fails business validation     |
| 429  | Too Many Requests     | Rate limit exceeded                           |
| 500  | Internal Server Error | Unexpected server-side failure                |
| 502  | Bad Gateway           | Invalid response from an upstream server      |
| 503  | Service Unavailable   | Service temporarily unable to handle requests |
One important distinction:

items: **403:** The requester is identified, but does not have permission for the operation.

blocks.text: The exact use of status codes should follow the API's documented conventions.
3.7 Stateless communication
HTTP is fundamentally a stateless request-response protocol.
This means the protocol itself does not automatically remember previous requests.
For example, after a student logs in, the next HTTP request does not automatically contain the context of the previous login request.
Applications maintain user identity through mechanisms such as:

items: Session identifiers stored in secure cookies.

blocks.text: The server validates the session or token on subsequent requests.
Stateless API design is useful because any suitable backend instance can process a request, provided it has access to the relevant shared state and authentication information.
However, stateless HTTP does not mean the application has no state. User accounts, database records, sessions, and other application state may still exist.
3.8 Synchronous and asynchronous communication
**Synchronous request-response:** The client sends a request and waits for the response before continuing with that operation.
Example: retrieving a student's profile.

Client → Backend → Database
Client ← Backend ← Database
**Asynchronous processing:** The application accepts or initiates work that continues independently, without requiring the client to wait for the entire operation to finish.
Example: generating a large course completion report.

Client
  |
  | Request report
  v
Backend API
  |
  | Submit background task
  v
Message Queue
  |
  v
Background Worker
  |
  v
Generate and store report
The client may initially receive a response such as:
It can later check the job's status or receive a notification when the report is ready.
This approach becomes important when operations are time-consuming or involve multiple services.
3.9 What happens when the server is unavailable?
Suppose a student submits a request while the backend is temporarily down.
Possible causes include:

items: A cloud infrastructure component is unavailable.

blocks.text: The client may receive a network error, a timeout, or an HTTP error response depending on where the failure occurs.
A well-designed system should handle these conditions deliberately. It should not leave the user with an unexplained blank screen.

Not every application needs all these infrastructure components. For example, a small application may receive traffic directly through its application server. Larger systems may have several networking and security layers before the request reaches the application.
4.2 Step 1: User action and frontend request
The student clicks the My Courses button.
The frontend executes an API call.
Example using JavaScript:
The frontend constructs a request and sends it to the backend.
At this point, the frontend is asking the backend for data. It is not deciding which private course records the student is authorized to receive.
4.3 Step 2: DNS resolution
Suppose the frontend sends the request to:
https://api.example.com/api/v1/me/courses
Before communicating with the server, the client needs to resolve the domain name.
DNS stands for Domain Name System.
DNS translates human-readable domain names into network addresses that computers can use.
Conceptually:

api.example.com
       |
       v
    DNS lookup
       |
       v
203.0.113.10
The IP address above is an illustrative documentation address, not a real server address.
DNS may involve caching at several levels, so a lookup does not necessarily require contacting a DNS server for every request.
4.4 Step 3: Establishing a network connection
For an HTTPS request, the client typically establishes a connection using TCP and negotiates TLS, depending on the transport protocol in use.
TLS (Transport Layer Security) protects communication by providing encryption, integrity, and server authentication through certificates.
The request can then travel over the secured connection.
Modern HTTP deployments may use HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, or HTTP/3. HTTP/3 uses QUIC rather than TCP as its transport.
The key learning point is that the request must travel through a network before it reaches the application.
4.5 Step 4: Edge server, reverse proxy, or load balancer
In a production deployment, the request may first reach an infrastructure layer.
Examples include:
**Reverse proxy:** Receives client requests and forwards them to the appropriate backend service. It may also handle TLS termination, request routing, and other infrastructure tasks.
**Load balancer:** Distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend instances.
**Web application firewall (WAF):** Applies security rules to incoming traffic and may block suspicious requests.
**CDN or edge network:** Helps deliver content and may route or process requests closer to users.
Example:

Incoming requests
                         |
                         v
                  Load Balancer
                   /         \
                  v           v
              Server A     Server B
                  |           |
                  +-----+-----+
                        |
                        v
                     Database
If Server A becomes unavailable, the load balancer may direct new requests to Server B, depending on its health checks and configuration.
A load balancer does not automatically make an application reliable. The backend instances, shared state, database, and other dependencies must also be designed for failure.
4.6 Step 5: Middleware processing
Middleware is code or infrastructure that processes a request before, during, or after the main route handler.
Common middleware responsibilities include:
Consider a logging middleware:
This records basic request information.
In a real system, logs should avoid exposing sensitive information such as passwords, access tokens, private personal data, or secret credentials.
Middleware allows common concerns to be implemented consistently instead of duplicating the same logic in every endpoint.
4.7 Step 6: Authentication
Authentication answers:
**Who is making this request?**
The application might receive an access token in the Authorization header.
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
The backend validates the credential.
Depending on the authentication mechanism, it may:

items: Check the token's issuer and audience.
Check whether the account has been disabled or revoked.

blocks.text: After successful authentication, the backend has a trusted identity associated with the request.
For illustration:

Authenticated User
------------------
User ID: user-501
Role: student
Status: active
These values should come from validated authentication context or trusted server-side data, not from arbitrary user-supplied fields.
4.8 Step 7: Authorization
Authentication and authorization solve different problems.
Authentication establishes identity.
Authorization decides what that identity is permitted to do.
For example:

items: A student can view their own course enrollments.
An instructor can view assigned course submissions.
An administrator may manage student records.
A student cannot access another student's private progress simply by changing an ID in the URL.

blocks.text: Suppose the API allows:
GET /api/v1/students/stu-1001/progress
A student might attempt to change the URL:
GET /api/v1/students/stu-1002/progress
The backend must verify that the requesting user is allowed to access `stu-1002`'s information.
Checking only that the user is logged in is not enough.
This is related to broken object-level authorization, a common API security risk.
A safer design for a student's own progress is often:
GET /api/v1/me/progress
The backend derives the student identity from the authenticated request context.
4.9 Step 8: Route matching and controller execution
The backend identifies which handler should process the request.
For example:
app.get("/api/v1/me/courses", getMyCourses);
The route associates a method and path with a controller function.
The controller is responsible for handling the HTTP-facing operation.
Example:
Notice that the controller obtains the student ID from the authenticated request context rather than trusting a student ID supplied by the frontend.
4.10 Step 9: Business logic execution
The service layer performs the application's actual business rules.
Example:
The exact implementation will vary, but the service layer should represent application behavior rather than merely forwarding database queries.
For example, a service may:

items: Determine whether a course is published.

blocks.text: Business logic should be implemented consistently so that the same rules apply regardless of which frontend or integration invokes the API.
4.11 Step 10: Database access
The backend needs to retrieve enrolled courses.
It may use a repository or data access layer to communicate with a database.
A simplified SQL query might look like:

SELECT
    courses.id,
    courses.title,
    enrollments.created_at
FROM enrollments
JOIN courses
    ON enrollments.course_id = courses.id
WHERE enrollments.student_id = ?
  AND enrollments.status = 'active'
  AND courses.status = 'published';
This query:
2. Joins them with course records.
3. Selects the specified student.
4. Filters for active enrollments.
5. Returns published courses.
The backend should use parameterized queries or a safe database access library rather than building SQL by concatenating untrusted input.
4.12 Step 11: Response construction
After the service receives the required data, the backend constructs a response.
Example:
The response includes only the information the client needs and is authorized to access.
The backend then sends an appropriate HTTP status and response body.
4.13 Step 12: Frontend receives and displays the response
The frontend receives the response, parses the JSON, and renders course cards.
It should handle several possibilities:
| Situation                     | Frontend behavior                               |
| Request is in progress        | Show a loading indicator                        |
| Request succeeds with data    | Render course cards                             |
| Request succeeds with no data | Display an empty-state message                  |
| Authentication expires        | Ask the user to authenticate again              |
| Permission denied             | Display an appropriate access message           |
| Server fails                  | Show a useful error and suitable retry behavior |
The complete lifecycle is now finished.
4.14 What can go wrong during request processing?
A backend engineer must think about failure at every stage.
| Stage          | Possible failure                | Possible handling                      |
| DNS            | Domain cannot be resolved       | Show connection failure                |
| Network        | Connection times out            | Controlled retry where appropriate     |
| TLS            | Certificate validation fails    | Reject insecure connection             |
| Middleware     | Rate limit exceeded             | Return 429                             |
| Authentication | Invalid or expired token        | Return 401                             |
| Authorization  | Access not permitted            | Return 403                             |
| Validation     | Invalid request                 | Return 400 or 422                      |
| Service        | Unexpected logic error          | Central error handling                 |
| Database       | Query or connection fails       | Log and handle safely                  |
| External API   | Third-party service unavailable | Timeout, fallback, or retry where safe |
| Response       | Serialization fails             | Return a controlled error              |
Do not expose internal stack traces, database credentials, SQL errors, or infrastructure details to ordinary API clients.
4.15 Understanding latency
Latency is the time taken for an operation or request to complete.
A request's overall latency may include:
\\[ T\_{\text{total}} = T\_{\text{network}} + T\_{\text{middleware}} + T\_{\text{application}} + T\_{\text{database}} + T\_{\text{external services}} \\]
This is a simplified model. Some operations happen in parallel, and measurements must be interpreted carefully.
Consider an illustrative request:
| Operation             | Time       |
| Network communication | 30 ms      |
| Authentication        | 5 ms       |
| Business logic        | 15 ms      |
| Database query        | 40 ms      |
| Response processing   | 10 ms      |
These are example measurements, not universal performance benchmarks.
A developer can use logs, metrics, traces, and database query analysis to identify which part of the lifecycle is slow.

5.1 What is an application server?
An application server is the environment or software component responsible for executing application logic and handling application operations.
In a web backend, it commonly accepts HTTP requests, invokes application code, and returns responses.
For example, a Java backend may run inside a JVM process using Spring Boot and an embedded web server.
A Node.js backend may run as a Node.js process using an HTTP framework.
A Python backend may run through an application server such as Gunicorn or Uvicorn, depending on the framework and application interface.
The terminology and implementation differ between ecosystems, but the underlying purpose is similar: execute backend code and serve application operations.
5.2 Server vs application server vs database server
These terms describe different roles.
| Component                  | Responsibility                                     |
| Physical or virtual server | Provides computing resources                       |
| Operating system           | Manages system resources and processes             |
| Runtime environment        | Executes the application's code                    |
| Application server         | Runs and serves application logic                  |
| Database server            | Manages database connections, queries, and storage |
| Reverse proxy              | Routes incoming requests to upstream systems       |
A single machine may run several of these components, or they may be deployed on different machines.
For example, a small project might run its application and database on one virtual machine. A larger system might host them separately.
5.3 What is a runtime environment?
A runtime environment provides what an application needs to execute.
It may provide:
Consider these ecosystems:
| Technology         | Runtime or execution environment                    |
| Java               | Java Virtual Machine (JVM)                          |
| JavaScript backend | Node.js                                             |
| Python             | Python interpreter and runtime                      |
| C#                 | .NET runtime                                        |
| Go                 | Native compiled executable with its runtime support |
A runtime is not the same as a framework.
For example:

items: Spring Boot is a framework used to build applications.

blocks.text: Similarly:
Understanding this distinction helps avoid confusing the language, runtime, framework, and hosting platform.
5.4 Application lifecycle
A typical backend application goes through these stages:
**1. Startup**
The application process starts. It loads configuration, initializes dependencies, and prepares the application.
**2. Initialization**
The application may connect to a database, register routes, configure middleware, and prepare services.
**3. Listening**
The server begins listening for incoming requests on a configured network address and port.
**4. Request processing**
The application receives and processes incoming requests.
**5. Shutdown**
When the process is stopped, a properly designed application performs graceful shutdown operations, such as finishing in-flight work and closing connections.
Example:
This is a minimal application. It starts an HTTP server and exposes a health endpoint.
A production server would need configuration, security controls, centralized error handling, graceful shutdown, monitoring, and proper dependency management.
5.5 Understanding ports
A port identifies a particular communication endpoint on a host.
For example:
http://localhost:3000
Here:
An application might run on port 3000 during development, while a reverse proxy forwards public traffic to it.
Ports allow multiple services to communicate on the same machine using different endpoints.
They are not the same as IP addresses: an IP address identifies a network interface or host address, while a port identifies an application-level communication endpoint.
5.6 Operating systems and processes
A backend application runs as an operating-system process.
The operating system manages:
A process may contain one or more threads, depending on the runtime and architecture.
Different runtimes handle concurrency in different ways.
For example:

items: Node.js commonly uses an event loop and asynchronous I/O.
Java applications commonly use multiple threads and can also use asynchronous or reactive models.
Python applications can use different process and thread models depending on the server and workload.
Go applications use goroutines for lightweight concurrent execution.

blocks.text: The important distinction is that a backend can process multiple requests without requiring one dedicated operating-system process for every request.
5.7 Concurrency and parallelism
These concepts are related but different.
**Concurrency** means organizing multiple tasks so that they can make progress during overlapping periods.
**Parallelism** means executing multiple tasks simultaneously, typically on multiple CPU cores or processing units.
Consider a backend handling 100 requests.
Many of these requests may spend time waiting for network or database operations. The server can use concurrency to work on other requests during those waits.
For CPU-intensive operations, parallel execution may be useful, depending on the runtime and deployment.
A backend engineer needs to understand the workload before choosing a concurrency strategy.
5.8 Application configuration
A backend application has environment-specific settings.
Examples include:

PORT
DATABASE_URL
JWT_SECRET
LOG_LEVEL
ENVIRONMENT
These values should be handled securely.
For example, a database password should not be committed to a public Git repository or included in frontend code.
A common approach is to use environment variables and a managed secrets system.
Different deployment environments may have different configurations:
| Setting         | Development                     | Production                       |
| Debugging       | Detailed developer output       | Restricted                       |
| Database        | Local or test database          | Production database              |
| Logging         | Developer-focused               | Structured operational logs      |
| Secrets         | Local environment configuration | Secure secrets management        |
| Error responses | Helpful development details     | Sanitized client-facing messages |
5.9 Infrastructure deployment models
Backend applications can run in several ways.
**Traditional server or virtual machine**
The application runs on a managed server or virtual machine. The operator manages the OS, runtime, deployment, security updates, and process lifecycle.
**Containers**
A container packages the application and its dependencies in a standardized execution environment. Docker is a widely used container technology.
Containers simplify packaging and deployment, but they still need orchestration, monitoring, networking, and resource management.
**Serverless computing**
The platform manages much of the server infrastructure. Developers deploy application code or functions, and the platform provisions execution resources as needed.
Serverless does not mean that servers do not exist. It means that the infrastructure management responsibility is largely abstracted from the application developer.
**Edge computing**
Application code runs in infrastructure distributed across geographically separated locations, often closer to users.
This can reduce network distance for suitable workloads, but data locality, execution limits, and architecture constraints must be considered.

As applications grow, one of the most important architectural decisions is how to organize application functionality and deploy it.
Two broad approaches are monolithic and distributed architectures.
6.1 What is a monolithic application?
A monolithic application is an application in which major application capabilities are developed and deployed as a single application unit.
A monolith can still have a well-structured codebase with separate modules.
For example, a student management backend could contain:

Student Management Backend
│
├── Authentication Module
├── Student Module
├── Instructor Module
├── Course Module
├── Enrollment Module
├── Payment Module
└── Reporting Module
        |
        v
     Database
All modules may execute inside the same application deployment.
For example, the authentication module, course module, and enrollment module may all run within one backend process or application deployment.
This does not mean that a monolith must have poorly organized code.
A well-designed monolith can use clear internal boundaries, interfaces, and separate business modules.
6.2 Advantages of monolithic architecture
**Simpler initial development:** Developers can work within one project and deploy one application unit.
**Simpler local testing:** Application modules can often be tested without setting up a distributed infrastructure.
**Straightforward communication:** Modules may communicate through in-process method calls instead of network requests.
**Simpler deployment:** There may be only one main application artifact to build and deploy.
**Potentially easier transactions:** When several operations share one database and transaction boundary, maintaining consistency can be simpler.
6.3 Disadvantages of monolithic architecture
**Scaling limitations:** If only one feature needs additional computing resources, the whole application may need to scale.
**Large codebase complexity:** Without good module boundaries, the codebase can become difficult to maintain.
**Shared deployment:** Changes to one module may require deploying the entire application.
**Shared failure domain:** A serious problem in one part of the application may affect the whole process.
**Team coordination:** Many developers working in one codebase may experience integration and deployment conflicts.
These disadvantages are not inevitable. A modular monolith can remain manageable for a substantial application.
6.4 What is distributed architecture?
A distributed application consists of multiple independently running components that communicate over a network to provide a complete system.
For example:

Frontend
                     |
                     v
                API Gateway
                     |
          +----------+----------+
          |          |          |
          v          v          v
       Auth       Course     Payment
       Service    Service    Service
          |          |          |
          v          v          v
       Auth DB    Course DB   Payment DB
Each service may have its own codebase, runtime, deployment lifecycle, and data storage strategy.
This is one possible architecture. Distributed systems may also share infrastructure or databases, although independent data ownership is often desirable in service-oriented designs.
6.5 What is a microservice?
A microservice is a small, independently deployable service organized around a business capability or domain boundary.
For example, a learning platform might have:
A microservice should have a clear responsibility and a well-defined communication contract.
The goal is not to create as many services as possible. The goal is to establish boundaries that support independent ownership, development, deployment, and scaling where needed.
6.6 Monolithic vs distributed architecture
| Factor                 | Monolithic                                        | Distributed                                       |
| Deployment             | One application unit                              | Multiple independently deployed components        |
| Internal communication | Often in-process                                  | Commonly network-based                            |
| Initial complexity     | Usually lower                                     | Usually higher                                    |
| Infrastructure needs   | Often simpler                                     | More infrastructure and operations                |
| Scaling                | Often scales the whole application                | Individual services can scale independently       |
| Failure handling       | Shared process may create a larger failure domain | Failures can be isolated, but may propagate       |
| Debugging              | Often simpler initially                           | Distributed tracing and correlation are important |
| Data management        | Often a shared database                           | May involve multiple data stores                  |
| Team ownership         | Shared application ownership                      | Can support independent domain teams              |
| Network dependency     | Lower within the application                      | Higher between services                           |
6.7 Distributed systems introduce new problems
Separating an application into services does not automatically make it faster, more secure, or more reliable.
Distributed architecture introduces additional challenges.
**Network failure:** A service may not be reachable even when the calling service is working.
**Timeouts:** A dependent service may take too long to respond.
**Partial failure:** Some services may work while others fail.
**Data consistency:** Changes across multiple databases may not happen as one atomic transaction.
**Communication overhead:** Network communication is generally more expensive than in-process calls.
**Observability:** A request may pass through several services, making logs and traces essential.
**Security:** Service-to-service communication must be authenticated and authorized.
**Operational complexity:** Developers must manage deployments, monitoring, service discovery, configuration, and dependencies across multiple components.
6.8 Synchronous service communication
Services can call each other through synchronous network requests.
Example:

Frontend
   |
   v
Course Service
   |
   | HTTP request
   v
Enrollment Service
   |
   v
Database
The Course Service waits for the Enrollment Service to return a response.
This is straightforward, but it introduces a dependency. If the Enrollment Service is slow or unavailable, the Course Service may also experience problems.
Timeouts, appropriate error handling, and careful dependency management are essential.
6.9 Asynchronous service communication
Services can also communicate through messages or events.
For example, after a student enrolls in a course:

Enrollment Service
       |
       | Publishes CourseEnrolled event
       v
    Message Broker
       |
       +----------------+
       |                |
       v                v
Notification       Analytics
Consumer            Consumer
       |                |
       v                v
Send email       Record event
The enrollment operation does not necessarily need to wait for email delivery or analytics processing.
This can reduce coupling between services.
However, asynchronous systems introduce challenges such as:
A message consumer should usually be designed so that processing a duplicate message does not create an incorrect result.
6.10 What is eventual consistency?
In a distributed system, separate components may not observe an update at exactly the same time.
Suppose a student enrolls in a course.
The enrollment service successfully saves the enrollment. The analytics service receives the event a short time later and updates its reporting data.
During that interval, the enrollment database knows about the new enrollment, but the analytics view may not yet include it.
The system is eventually consistent if the related data converges to the correct state after the updates are successfully propagated, under the system's assumptions.
This is different from strong consistency, where a system promises stronger guarantees about when reads observe committed updates.
6.11 When should you choose a monolith?
A modular monolith is often a strong starting choice when:

items: The domain boundaries are still evolving.

blocks.text: 6.12 When should you consider distributed services?
Distributed services become worth considering when:

items: Different business domains need independent development and deployment.
Different components have substantially different technology or operational needs.
The organization can support the additional infrastructure and engineering complexity.

blocks.text: A useful principle is:
**Start with the simplest architecture that satisfies the real requirements, then introduce distribution when there is a measurable reason to do so.**
6.13 Example: Evolving a learning platform
A learning platform begins as one modular backend:

Learning Platform
├── Users
├── Courses
├── Enrollments
├── Progress
└── Notifications
As usage grows, the application may experience a large amount of asynchronous notification traffic.
The engineering team could extract notifications into a separate service while keeping the rest of the application as a modular monolith.
Later, if payment processing needs separate compliance and operational boundaries, the payment functionality may be separated as well.
This demonstrates an important idea: architecture can evolve incrementally. You do not need to start with microservices to build a system that can eventually support them.

7.1 What is a backend architecture pattern?
An architecture pattern is a reusable way of organizing application components and responsibilities.
Patterns help developers solve recurring design problems.
For example:

items: How should the backend separate HTTP handling from business logic?
Where should database operations be implemented?
How should application dependencies be managed?
How can business rules be tested independently?

blocks.text: There is no single pattern that is ideal for every backend.
The right approach depends on application complexity, team size, requirements, and operational constraints.
7.2 Layered architecture
Layered architecture separates an application into logical layers, each with a specific responsibility.
A common backend implementation has:
2. Application or service layer.
3. Domain or business logic layer.
4. Data access layer.
5. Database or external storage.
Illustration:

HTTP Request
                |
                v
        Presentation Layer
       Routes / Controllers
                |
                v
        Application Layer
             Services
                |
                v
          Domain Layer
          Business Rules
                |
                v
        Data Access Layer
          Repositories
                |
                v
             Database
**Presentation layer:** Receives requests, interprets HTTP inputs, and creates responses.
**Application layer:** Coordinates the steps required to execute a use case.
**Domain layer:** Represents business concepts, rules, and domain behavior.
**Data access layer:** Handles persistence and retrieves data from storage.
These layers can be combined or named differently in different frameworks.
Example: Student enrollment
A student requests enrollment in a course.
The controller receives the request and passes the relevant information to the enrollment service.
The service checks whether:

items: The student is not already enrolled.
Any relevant business requirements are satisfied.

blocks.text: The repository saves the enrollment.
The controller returns the result.
**Why use layered architecture?**
It improves separation of concerns, testability, and maintainability. For example, business rules can be tested without sending a real HTTP request.
A possible drawback is unnecessary abstraction: very small applications may not need many layers or interfaces.
7.3 Model-View-Controller (MVC)
MVC is a pattern that separates an application's concerns into three conceptual parts:
**Model:** Represents application data and, depending on the implementation, related business behavior.
**View:** Presents information to the user.
**Controller:** Handles user input or requests and coordinates the appropriate operations.
In a traditional server-rendered web application, the flow might be:

User Request

     v
 Controller
     |
     v
   Model
     |
     v
 Database
     |
     v
 Controller
     |
     v
    View
     |
     v
HTML Response
In API-only applications, MVC concepts may still be used, but the response is often JSON rather than a rendered HTML page.
For example:

GET /api/v1/students
          |
          v
  Student Controller
          |
          v
   Student Model / Service
          |
          v
       Database
          |
          v
    JSON Response
MVC helps clarify responsibilities, but a complex application may need additional service and repository layers.
7.4 Clean Architecture
Clean Architecture is an approach that emphasizes separation of business rules from external technology details.
The central idea is that important application policies should not depend directly on specific frameworks, databases, or user interface implementations.
One possible conceptual structure:

External Systems
     Web / Database / APIs
               |
               v
       Interface Adapters
    Controllers / Presenters
               |
               v
      Application Use Cases
               |
               v
         Domain Entities
The exact structure can vary. The important concept is the direction of dependencies.
**Business logic should be protected from unnecessary dependence on frameworks and infrastructure.**
For example, an enrollment rule should not need to know whether the request came through Express, Spring Boot, or a mobile API.
Similarly, the business rule should not require a particular database technology to exist in its design.
This makes the core rules easier to test and can make infrastructure changes easier.
However, Clean Architecture also adds abstractions and design discipline. Applying all its layers to a very small application can create unnecessary complexity.
7.5 Repository pattern
The Repository pattern separates data access from the business logic that uses the data.
Instead of directly placing SQL queries throughout the application, the service calls a repository.
Example:

const student = await studentRepository
  .findById(studentId);
The service does not need to know exactly how the repository retrieves the record.

**Benefits:** Data access is centralized, and tests can substitute a mock repository.
**Trade-off:** Creating repository abstractions around every trivial database operation can add unnecessary code. Use them when they improve separation or testability.
7.6 Service-oriented architecture
Service-oriented architecture (SOA) organizes application functionality into services that provide defined business capabilities.
A service exposes functionality through a documented interface.
For example:
Services may be deployed together or separately. SOA is a broader architectural idea and is not synonymous with microservices.
Microservices are one style of service-oriented architecture with an emphasis on smaller, independently deployable services.
7.7 Event-driven architecture
Event-driven architecture organizes some system behavior around events.
An event is a record that something meaningful has happened.
Examples:

StudentRegistered
CoursePublished
StudentEnrolled
AssignmentSubmitted
PaymentCompleted
An event producer publishes an event, and one or more consumers react to it.
Example:

Student Registration
         |
         v
     User Service
         |
         v
 Publishes StudentRegistered
         |
         v
    Message Broker
      /       \
     v         v
Notification  Analytics
  Consumer    Consumer
This is useful when multiple parts of the application need to react to the same event without requiring the original operation to call each system directly.
For example, after a student's account is created:

items: A notification consumer sends a welcome email.
An analytics consumer records a registration event.
A recommendation consumer may prepare suggested courses.

blocks.text: The registration operation should not necessarily fail just because an analytics consumer is temporarily unavailable.
However, the system must implement message delivery, retry, and duplicate-handling strategies carefully.
7.8 Choosing between architecture patterns
| Pattern            | Main goal                                             | Suitable situation                                    |
| Layered            | Separate responsibilities into layers                 | Most conventional backend applications                |
| MVC                | Separate model, controller, and presentation concerns | Web applications                                      |
| Clean Architecture | Isolate business logic from infrastructure            | Complex domains with long-term maintenance needs      |
| Repository         | Separate data access from business operations         | Systems with meaningful persistence abstraction       |
| Service-oriented   | Organize functionality around service capabilities    | Systems with clear service boundaries                 |
| Event-driven       | React to events asynchronously                        | Notifications, workflows, analytics, and integrations |
These patterns are not mutually exclusive.
For example, a backend can use layered architecture internally, MVC-style controllers for HTTP requests, repositories for data access, and event-driven communication for notifications.
7.9 A practical architecture example
Consider a Student Management Backend.
A reasonable initial design is a modular monolith with layered organization:

Student Management Backend
│
├── API Layer
│   ├── Student Routes
│   ├── Course Routes

├── Service Layer
│   ├── Student Service
│   ├── Course Service
│   └── Enrollment Service
│
├── Repository Layer
│   ├── Student Repository
│   ├── Course Repository
│   └── Enrollment Repository
│
├── Domain
│   ├── Student Rules
│   ├── Course Rules
│   └── Enrollment Rules
│
└── Infrastructure
    ├── Database
    ├── Logging
    └── External Integrations
This provides a clear foundation without introducing distributed-system complexity prematurely.

sections.title: 8. How to Design a Backend Application from Requirements

blocks.text: This lesson brings the previous concepts together.
A backend should not be designed by randomly creating APIs and tables. The engineering process starts by understanding the problem the application needs to solve.
8.1 Step 1: Understand the application requirements
Suppose an institute wants a Student Management System.
The institute wants to:
Before writing code, translate these requests into clearly defined requirements.
There are two important categories.
**Functional requirements** describe what the application must do.
Examples:

items: The system must allow administrators to register students.
Students must be able to view their enrolled courses.
Instructors must be able to record attendance.
Students must be able to submit assignments.
Administrators must be able to generate enrollment reports.

blocks.text: **Non-functional requirements** describe the quality attributes and constraints under which the system operates.
Examples:

items: Only authorized users can access protected operations.
Common API requests should respond within an agreed performance target.
The system should support a defined number of concurrent users.
Data must be backed up regularly.
The system should recover gracefully from service failures.

blocks.text: Functional requirements describe capabilities. Non-functional requirements describe qualities and operational constraints.
8.2 Step 2: Identify the users and their roles
An application has different types of users, and they may have different permissions.
For the Student Management System:
| Role          | Typical capabilities                                 |
| Administrator | Manage students, instructors, courses, and reports   |
| Instructor    | Manage assigned courses, attendance, and assignments |
| Student       | View own profile, courses, attendance, and progress  |
This is an initial role model. Production applications may need more granular permissions.
For example, an instructor may only manage courses assigned to them. A student may only view their own attendance records.
8.3 Step 3: Identify the major business entities
An entity represents an important concept in the application's domain.
The Student Management System may contain the following entities:
**Student:** A person enrolled in the institute.
**Instructor:** A person responsible for teaching or managing courses.
**Course:** A learning program offered by the institute.
**Enrollment:** The relationship between a student and a course.
**Attendance:** A record of a student's attendance for a session.
**Assignment:** Work given to students.
**Submission:** A student's submitted response to an assignment.
**User:** An account used to authenticate and access the system.
A common mistake is creating one enormous table for every type of information. Separate entities help model relationships and maintain data integrity.
8.4 Step 4: Understand entity relationships
An entity relationship model describes how the data entities are connected.
Consider these relationships:

items: One student can have multiple enrollments.
One course can have multiple enrollments.
One instructor can teach multiple courses.
One course can contain multiple assignments.
One assignment can have multiple student submissions.
One student can have multiple attendance records.

blocks.text: An enrollment entity is particularly important because students and courses have a many-to-many relationship.
A student can enroll in many courses, and a course can contain many students.
Instead of storing multiple course IDs inside a student record, create an enrollment table to represent that relationship.
8.5 Step 5: Design the database structure
A simplified relational database might look like this:
**users**
| Column        | Type      | Purpose                                             |
| id            | UUID      | Primary key                                         |
| email         | VARCHAR   | Login identity                                      |
| password_hash | VARCHAR   | Password hash, when password authentication is used |
| role          | VARCHAR   | Account role                                        |
| status        | VARCHAR   | Account status                                      |
| created_at    | TIMESTAMP | Creation time                                       |
**students**
| Column            | Type    | Purpose                 |
| id                | UUID    | Primary key             |
| user_id           | UUID    | Associated user account |
| full_name         | VARCHAR | Student name            |
| phone             | VARCHAR | Contact number          |
| enrollment_number | VARCHAR | Institute identifier    |
**instructors**
| Column     | Type    | Purpose                 |
| id         | UUID    | Primary key             |
| user_id    | UUID    | Associated user account |
| full_name  | VARCHAR | Instructor name         |
| department | VARCHAR | Department              |
**courses**
| Column        | Type    | Purpose             |
| id            | UUID    | Primary key         |
| instructor_id | UUID    | Assigned instructor |
| title         | VARCHAR | Course title        |
| description   | TEXT    | Course description  |
| status        | VARCHAR | Publication status  |
**enrollments**
| Column      | Type      | Purpose           |
| id          | UUID      | Primary key       |
| student_id  | UUID      | Student reference |
| course_id   | UUID      | Course reference  |
| status      | VARCHAR   | Enrollment state  |
| enrolled_at | TIMESTAMP | Enrollment time   |
**attendance**
| Column       | Type    | Purpose           |
| id           | UUID    | Primary key       |
| student_id   | UUID    | Student reference |
| course_id    | UUID    | Course reference  |

A few important constraints:

items: A unique constraint on `(student_id, course_id)` can prevent duplicate active enrollment records, depending on the enrollment lifecycle design.
Frequently queried fields may need indexes.

blocks.text: 8.6 Step 6: Design the API endpoints
Once requirements, entities, and relationships are understood, define the API contract.
An initial API structure could be:
| Method | Endpoint                              | Purpose                                      |
| POST   | `/api/v1/auth/login`                  | Authenticate a user                          |
| GET    | `/api/v1/students`                    | List students                                |
| POST   | `/api/v1/students`                    | Register a student                           |
| GET    | `/api/v1/students/:id`                | Retrieve a student                           |
| PATCH  | `/api/v1/students/:id`                | Update student information                   |
| DELETE | `/api/v1/students/:id`                | Delete or deactivate a student               |
| GET    | `/api/v1/courses`                     | List courses                                 |
| POST   | `/api/v1/courses`                     | Create a course                              |
| GET    | `/api/v1/courses/:id`                 | Retrieve course information                  |
| POST   | `/api/v1/courses/:id/enrollments`     | Enroll a student                             |
| GET    | `/api/v1/me/courses`                  | Retrieve the authenticated student's courses |
| POST   | `/api/v1/attendance`                  | Record attendance                            |
| POST   | `/api/v1/assignments/:id/submissions` | Submit an assignment                         |
| GET    | `/api/v1/reports/enrollments`         | Retrieve an enrollment report                |
An API endpoint is more than a URL. It should also have a defined contract describing:

items: Pagination and filtering behavior, where relevant.

blocks.text: For example:
**Create a course**

POST /api/v1/courses
Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
Content-Type: application/json
Request:
Expected success response:
The backend should verify that the authenticated user has permission to create a course. It should not assume every logged-in user is an administrator or instructor.
8.7 Step 7: Define the business rules
Before implementation, identify rules that affect application behavior.
Examples:
**Student registration**

items: Required personal information must be present.
Only authorized users can register students.

blocks.text: **Course creation**

items: Only authorized users can create or edit courses.
An instructor may only edit courses within their assigned permissions.

blocks.text: **Enrollment**

items: The course must be available for enrollment.
A duplicate enrollment must be prevented.
Enrollment status must follow the application's rules.

blocks.text: **Assignment submission**

items: The student must be enrolled in the relevant course.
The submission deadline must be checked.
Uploaded file types and sizes must be validated.
Submission records must be linked to the correct student and assignment.

blocks.text: These rules belong in trusted backend logic. The frontend may help users avoid mistakes, but the backend must enforce them.
8.8 Step 8: Choose the architecture
For this initial application, a modular monolith is a reasonable starting design.
Why?

items: The requirements form one related application.
Multiple modules need to work with shared student and course information.
There may be a small development team.
One deployment unit is easier to operate initially.
The application does not yet demonstrate a need for independently deployed services.

The important thing is to keep related functionality together and maintain clear responsibility boundaries.
8.9 Step 9: Plan security
Security needs to be part of the original design, not something added after development.
The application should consider:
**Authentication:** How will users establish their identities?
**Authorization:** Which users can perform which actions?
**Password security:** Passwords should be hashed using an appropriate password-hashing algorithm, not stored in plaintext.
**Transport security:** Use HTTPS for production communication.
**Input validation:** Validate every untrusted input at the backend boundary.
**SQL injection protection:** Use parameterized queries or safe data access libraries.
**Rate limiting:** Restrict abusive or excessive requests where appropriate.
**Sensitive data protection:** Do not return private information unless it is necessary and authorized.
**Audit logging:** Record important administrative actions where required.
**File security:** Validate file type, size, access permissions, and storage handling.
Security decisions should be reflected in the database, API design, middleware, and application services.
8.10 Step 10: Plan testing and reliability
A backend design should include a testing strategy.
| Test type          | What it checks            | Example                                      |
| Unit test          | Individual logic          | Enrollment rule rejects a duplicate          |
| Integration test   | Interacting components    | Service correctly reads from database        |
| API test           | HTTP endpoint behavior    | Creating a course returns 201                |
| Authorization test | Access restrictions       | Student cannot access another student's data |
| Performance test   | Handling load             | Course list under expected concurrent usage  |
| Security test      | Potential vulnerabilities | Input validation and access control          |
| End-to-end test    | Complete user workflow    | Register, enroll, and view a course          |

The institute currently manages student details, courses, attendance, assignment submissions, and instructor information using spreadsheets and manual processes.
